title: Hierarchical, DBSCAN & Gaussian Mixtures
html:
Beyond k-means: hierarchical clustering builds a tree of merges, DBSCAN finds dense regions of any shape and labels noise, and Gaussian mixtures give soft, elliptical clusters with probabilities.

Hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering

Start with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merge the two closest clusters until one remains. The merge history is a dendrogram; cutting it at a height (or asking for n_clusters) gives the clusters.

LinkageDistance between clustersTends to produce
SingleClosest pair of pointsLong chains; finds non-convex shapes but is fooled by bridges of noise
CompleteFarthest pair of pointsCompact clusters of similar diameter
AverageMean of all pairwise distancesA compromise
WardIncrease in total within-cluster varianceCompact, similar-sized clusters (like k-means) — the default

No need to pick k up front and the dendrogram is informative — but the standard algorithm needs O(n²) memory, so it suits thousands of points, not millions.

DBSCAN — density-based clustering

A point is a core point if at least min_samples points (itself included) lie within distance eps. Clusters are chains of core points plus the border points they reach; everything else is noise (label −1). No k needed, any shape works:

  • Choosing eps: plot each point's distance to its min_samples-th nearest neighbour, sorted; pick the knee (the “k-distance plot”).
  • Struggles when clusters have very different densities (one eps can't fit all) and in high dimensions. HDBSCAN (sklearn.cluster.HDBSCAN) handles varying densities and needs only a minimum cluster size.
  • Scale features first — eps is a distance.

Gaussian mixture models

p(x) = Σₖ πₖ · N(x | μₖ, Σₖ) fitted by expectation–maximisation (EM)

A GMM assumes the data comes from k Gaussian blobs with their own means, covariances (so elliptical shapes and different sizes) and weights. EM alternates between computing each point's membership probabilities (E-step) and re-estimating the blobs from them (M-step). It gives soft assignments; k-means is roughly the special case with equal spherical covariances and hard assignments.

Which clustering method?

MethodNeeds k?Cluster shapesNoise handlingScales to
k-meansYesSpherical, similar sizeNone — outliers pull centroidsMillions (mini-batch)
AgglomerativeNo (cut the tree)Depends on linkagePoorThousands
DBSCAN / HDBSCANNoArbitraryLabels noise pointsLarge, low-dimensional data
Gaussian mixtureYes (choose with BIC)Ellipses of any orientationLow-probability points can be flaggedMedium
What is the difference between k-means and a Gaussian mixture model?

k-means makes hard assignments and implicitly assumes spherical clusters of equal size. A GMM models each cluster as a Gaussian with its own mean, covariance and weight, gives soft (probabilistic) assignments, and can fit elliptical clusters; it's trained with EM and k can be chosen with BIC.

When would you use DBSCAN?

When clusters have arbitrary shapes, the number of clusters is unknown, and you want outliers labelled as noise — e.g. GPS points into places. Avoid it when densities vary a lot (use HDBSCAN) or in high dimensions.

What does the linkage choose in hierarchical clustering?

How the distance between two clusters is measured — closest pair (single), farthest pair (complete), average of all pairs (average) or the increase in within-cluster variance (Ward). It changes the shapes of clusters the method prefers.
